y-m-31-01.title: Finding where Minseo's solution went wrong
y-m-31-01.topic: Checking a solution about variance and standard deviation
y-m-31-01.goal: Find the line that went wrong in a variance and standard deviation solution, say a clue that the result looks strange without recalculating all the way through, and make another data set with the same mean and variance yourself.
y-m-31-01.material: The quiz scores (points) of the 5 students in Minseo's group are 4, 7, 5, 8, 11. To find how spread out this data is, Minseo solved it as below. One line of Minseo's solution is off. These 5 students are all of the people being surveyed, so the variance is found by dividing by 5.
y-m-31-01.thinking.0: Finding the error by checking the reason for each line of the solution
y-m-31-01.thinking.1: Checking whether the size of the result is plausible
y-m-31-01.thinking.2: Making another data set that satisfies all the conditions
y-m-31-01.prereq.0: The meaning of mean and deviation (grade 8)
y-m-31-01.prereq.1: Definitions of variance and standard deviation: the mean of the squared deviations is the variance, and its positive square root is the standard deviation (grade 9). The data in this task are the scores of all students, so we divide by the number of data values.
y-m-31-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line that went wrong in Minseo's solution.
y-m-31-01.s.s1.hint.0: Line by line, point out how the number in each line came from the number in the line right before it.
y-m-31-01.s.s1.hint.1: Recalculate the numbers of each line yourself, and look at how the number in the last line relates to the number in the line right before it.
y-m-31-01.s.s1.line.2: The sum of deviations = -3+0-2+1+4 = 0, so the mean was found correctly.
y-m-31-01.s.s1.explain: The line that went wrong is line 6. Up to line 5, each number came correctly from the earlier line. The negative deviations in line 2 are normal values that arise because the scores are lower than the mean, and the deviations summing to 0 in line 3 always happens when the mean is found correctly. Line 6 carried the variance 6 straight over as the standard deviation. The standard deviation is not the variance but the positive square root of the variance, so it is √6 (about 2.4 points).
y-m-31-01.s.s2.prompt: Before recalculating line 6, choose all the clues that make this line worth doubting.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.hint.0: Put the size of the standard deviation side by side with the 5 deviations -3, 0, -2, 1, 4 and compare.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write the units of the variance and the standard deviation, and check whether the two units are the same.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.o.a: Negative values like -3 and -2 are mixed in among the deviations.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.r.a: A deviation is negative for a score lower than the mean. Since they are squared and added, having negatives does not make the solution wrong.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.o.b: The standard deviation 6 is greater than the largest deviation size 4.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.r.b: You turned your attention to the fact that the typical size of the deviations cannot be greater than the largest deviation. It is a good check that compared the size of the result with the data.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.o.c: There are 5 data values, and dividing by 5 when finding the variance seems wrong.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.r.c: All 5 are the people being surveyed, so dividing by the count 5 is this task's convention. This line is not a problem.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.o.d: The variance and the standard deviation are both 6, but the units are points² and points.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.r.d: This is a good check that found it strange that two quantities with different units are written with the same number. You recalled that the unit changes when going from variance to standard deviation.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.o.e: It feels strange that adding up all the deviations gave 0.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.r.e: The sum of the deviations is always 0 if the mean was found correctly. Getting 0 is actually a sign that the earlier steps are right.
y-m-31-01.s.s2.explain: You can have doubts in two ways without redoing the solution from the start. First, the standard deviation is a representative value of the size of the deviations, so it cannot be greater than the largest deviation size (here 4), but 6 came out. Second, the variance (points²) and the standard deviation (points) have different units, but the same number is written. The negative deviations, dividing by 5, and the deviations summing to 0 are all normal.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.prompt: Make 5 scores that differ from the original data (4, 5, 7, 8, 11) but have a mean of 7 points and a variance of 6. Scores are integers from 0 to 15, and the same score may appear several times. Make 2 different data sets. (Ones that only differ in order are the same data.)
y-m-31-01.s.s3.hint.0: First decide what the sum of the 5 must be, and place the scores so that the distances from the mean (deviations) are spread between -3 and 4.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.hint.1: Once you have decided the scores, square the deviations and check whether their total is 30.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.ok.c1: The scores are integers from 0 to 15.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.fail.c1: Make the scores integers from 0 to 15.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.fail.c2: The mean is not 7 points. Check the sum of the 5.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.fail.c3: The variance is not 6. Check the total of the squared deviations.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.ok.c4: It is data different from the original data.
y-m-31-01.s.s3.fail.c4: It is the same data as the original data (4, 5, 7, 8, 11).
y-m-31-01.s.s3.explain: For example, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10 has a sum of 35 and a sum of squared deviations of 16+1+0+4+9=30, so the variance is 6. 4, 4, 9, 9, 9 and 5, 5, 5, 10, 10 also satisfy the same conditions. Even if the mean and the variance are the same, the data can be different from each other.

y-m-31-02.title: Ice cream and swimming accidents: how far can we go in what we say?
y-m-31-02.goal: Read the way two variables increase together, revise your judgment about 'the cause' each time new data arrives, and tell apart what can and cannot be said from correlation alone.
y-m-31-02.material: In Seaside Town, the monthly ice cream sales (in thousands) and the number of swimming accidents (cases) at the beach were recorded from March to August. By month, (sales, accidents) are March (9, 2), April (14, 3), May (20, 5), June (26, 7), July (34, 10), and August (36, 11). Imagine drawing a scatter plot with the sales on the horizontal axis and the number of accidents on the vertical axis.
y-m-31-02.thinking.0: Reading correlation from the shape of a scatter plot
y-m-31-02.thinking.1: Revising your judgment and how sure you are after seeing new data
y-m-31-02.prereq.0: Telling apart positive correlation, negative correlation, and no correlation by looking at a scatter plot (middle school grade 8 to 9 level)
y-m-31-02.s.s1.prompt: Data is added one piece at a time. Each time, choose what you think.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, pick two or three numbers from the table and compare side by side how the other moves when one gets bigger.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether the newly revealed information changes the fact that they 'move together' or changes the way of explaining that fact.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.info: You only know the (sales, accidents) values for the 6 months above.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: What shape will the 6 points on the scatter plot take?
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.after: The larger the sales, the larger the number of accidents tends to be, so the points head toward the upper right. They are gathered very close together, so the correlation is strong.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The points go down to the lower right, and in months with many sales there tend to be fewer accidents
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Look at the table again. Check whether the number of accidents gets bigger or smaller when the sales get bigger.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: All the points lie exactly on one line
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: When sales go up by 5 from 9 to 14, accidents go up by 1, and when sales go up by 6 from 14 to 20, accidents go up by 2, so the amount of increase is not constant. They are just gathered around a line, not exactly on one line.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The points go up to the upper right, and in months with many sales there tend to be many accidents too
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You read that sales and the number of accidents tend to get bigger together, that is, a positive correlation.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The points are scattered with no clear direction
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Compare the two points for March and August. To say there is no direction is not right, since sales and the number of accidents move together.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.info: An official at city hall says, 'Ice cream sales and the number of accidents increase together like this, so if ice cream sales are reduced, swimming accidents will go down too.'
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: What do you think about this statement?
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.after: Just because you saw things increase together (correlation), you cannot say that one is the cause of the other. There may be a hidden factor, and to confirm whether it is a cause, you need another method.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is hard to call it a cause just from increasing together. Another reason may affect both
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You told correlation and causation apart, and even thought about the possibility of another hidden factor.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The correlation is this clear, so you can say that if ice cream sales are reduced, swimming accidents will go down too
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Increasing together and one causing the other are different facts. This table cannot tell you whether accidents would really decrease if sales were reduced.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The table alone cannot tell, so we have to reduce sales and see whether accidents change
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You did not decide on a cause from the observed data alone and thought of a way to verify. Also think about the point that conditions must be carefully controlled.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is hard to even believe there is a correlation between sales and the number of accidents, and the numbers in the table came out that way by chance
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The 6 points in the table clearly show a tendency to increase together. The fact that there is a correlation and the interpretation that it is a cause are different matters.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.info: You looked up the average temperature (°C) for the same months. March 6, April 12, May 18, June 23, July 27, August 28. Both temperature and accidents, and temperature and sales, form shapes that increase together.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: Add this data and sort out your thoughts.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.after: Temperature moves together with both sales and accidents, so you can explain why the two values increased together by temperature. Still, to assert that sales have no effect at all on accidents, you need more data or experiments.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It has been proved for certain by this table that temperature is the cause of accidents, so there is nothing more to look into
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Temperature also only shows correlation. There may be other factors besides weather, such as the number of visitors, so it is too early to call it 'proof'.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Once we knew the temperature, the correlation between sales and the number of accidents disappeared, so the two are unrelated
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Even when the temperature data is added, the shape of the points for sales and accidents stays the same. The correlation remains and only the interpretation changes.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Even with the temperature data added, the official's first statement that reducing sales would reduce accidents is still believable as it is
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: A factor like temperature that can affect both has appeared. The basis for believing the first statement as it is has become weaker.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Temperature may have affected both. But it is too early to assert that sales are unrelated to accidents
y-m-31-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You reflected the new data and also adjusted how sure you are appropriately.
y-m-31-02.s.s1.reflect: In step 2, how did my thinking change after meeting the data in step 3? If my first thought stayed the same, tell how the new data changed how sure I am.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.prompt: Write a reply to the city hall official in 2 to 3 sentences. Give at least one number from the table as evidence, and state how you see the proposal that 'if sales are reduced, accidents will go down'.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.hint.0: In the table, pick the month with the fewest sales and the month with the most sales and write the number of accidents and the temperature side by side.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.hint.1: First write in one sentence what would have to be confirmed for the official's proposal to be right.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. Unlike the proposal you mentioned, the table shows ...
y-m-31-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Are the numbers or evidence I gave actually values in the table?
y-m-31-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did I write distinguishing 'increase together' from 'is the cause'?
y-m-31-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did I propose to the official what to check in the future?
y-m-31-02.s.s2.model.0: In March, sales were 9 with 2 accidents, and in August, 36 with 11, so the two increased together. But when the temperature rises, both values can increase together, so it is hard to assert that reducing sales would reduce accidents.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.model.1: The table shows that in hotter months, both sales and accidents are higher (August temperature 28 degrees, 11 accidents). There is not yet evidence that ice cream is the cause, so I think it would be good to decide after checking other factors such as the number of visitors.
y-m-31-02.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that used temperature as evidence and proposed further checking.

y-m-31-03.title: The mean went up but the middle stayed the same
y-m-31-03.topic: Different changes in the mean and the median
y-m-31-03.goal: Make, according to the conditions yourself, a case where only some scores change so that the mean changes while the median stays the same, and explain that the two values tell different things.
y-m-31-03.material: The performance assessment scores (points) of 5 students were 60, 65, 70, 75, 80. Both the mean and the median are 70 points. The grading criteria were revised, and only the scores of the student who had 60 points and the student who had 80 points were re-graded. Call the new scores a points and b points (integers from 0 to 100), and the scores of the other three students (65 points, 70 points, 75 points) stay the same. After the re-grading, the mean went up by 4 points or more from 70 points, but the median was still 70 points.
y-m-31-03.thinking.0: Sorting out what must hold from the conditions and what does not
y-m-31-03.thinking.1: Making several cases that satisfy all the conditions
y-m-31-03.thinking.2: Choosing the representative value that fits the situation and giving the reason
y-m-31-03.prereq.0: The meaning of mean and median and how to find them (grades 7 to 8)
y-m-31-03.prereq.1: When 5 data values are arranged by size, the middle value is the median
y-m-31-03.s.s1.prompt: In the situation above, choose all the statements that must be true.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.hint.0: First calculate by at least how many points the sum of the 5 students' scores must have increased if the mean went up by 4 points.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.hint.1: Make a table showing, when the other three scores 65, 70, 75 and a, b are arranged by size, on which side of 70 a and b must lie for 70 to come in the middle.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.o.a: The sum of the new scores a and b is 160 or more.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.r.a: You used the fact that the mean went up by 4 points so the sum of the 5 went up by 20 points or more. The sum of the original two scores is 140 points.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.o.b: The median stayed the same, so the sum of the two changed scores is also the same as before, 140 points.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.r.b: The median is the value in the middle position, so it can stay the same even if the sum of the two scores changes. The mean going up means the sum changed.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.o.c: The number of students with 70 points or more increased from 3.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.r.c: You can make cases like (60→60, 80→100) where the number of students with 70 points or more is still 3. You cannot say it necessarily increased.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.o.d: At least one of the two newly graded scores is 90 points or more.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.r.d: The sum is 160 or more but one score must be 70 or less, so this is good reasoning that worked out how large the other score has to be.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.o.e: Both the student who had 60 points and the student who had 80 points have new scores higher than before.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.r.e: Of the two changed scores, one may stay the same or even go down. Think about whether there is a case that satisfies the conditions even if the student who had 60 points stays at 60.
y-m-31-03.s.s1.explain: The mean went up by 4 points, so the sum went up by 20 or more and a+b is 160 or more. For the median to stay 70, one of a and b must be 70 or less and the other 70 or more. If one is 70 or less, the other must be 90 or more for the sum to exceed 160. Even if one student's score stays the same, as in (60, 100), the conditions are satisfied, so a (the statement that the score of the student who had 60 points went up) is not necessarily true.
y-m-31-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different cases of new scores (a, b) that fit the conditions. a and b are integers from 0 to 100, and after the re-grading, the mean must go up by 4 points or more from 70 points and the median must stay at 70 points. (Swapping a and b is the same case.)
y-m-31-03.s.s2.hint.0: Test a few pairs for which 70 comes in the middle when the 5 scores 65, 70, 75 and a, b are arranged by size.
y-m-31-03.s.s2.hint.1: Decide one score so that the sum a+b is 160 or more, and adjust the other score. Remember that cases that only differ in order are counted as one.
y-m-31-03.s.s2.var.a: New score of the student who had 60 points
y-m-31-03.s.s2.var.b: New score of the student who had 80 points
y-m-31-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The scores are integers from 0 to 100.
y-m-31-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Make the scores integers from 0 to 100.
y-m-31-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The mean went up by 4 points or more.
y-m-31-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The mean did not go up by 4 points or more. Check the sum of the 5.
y-m-31-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The median is not 70 points. Check the middle value when the 5 are arranged by size.
y-m-31-03.s.s2.explain: For example, (60, 100) has a sum of 160, and arranged by size it is 60, 65, 70, 75, 100, so the median is 70. (70, 90) and (65, 95) are also the same. (80, 80) has a mean of 74 points but the median changes to 75 points, and (100, 100) also makes the median 75 points. The cases that fit the conditions are pairs where one score is around 60 to 70, the other is around 90 to 100, and the sum is 160 or more.
y-m-31-03.s.s3.prompt: You want to tell parents in a notice, in one or two sentences, how this class's scores changed. Write which of the mean and the median to use and how, with the reason.
y-m-31-03.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one of the cases you made, write all 5 students' new scores, and count how many students' scores changed.
y-m-31-03.s.s3.hint.1: For each of the mean and the median, write one line saying 'what you can know from this value alone' and compare.
y-m-31-03.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. In the notice, I will use ... because ...
y-m-31-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you think about whether the value I chose tells 'whether the scores of the students in this class went up overall'?
y-m-31-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think about what gets hidden if you use only one of the mean and the median?
y-m-31-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you give numbers (scores) in the reason?
y-m-31-03.s.s3.model.0: I will write the mean of 74 points and the median of 70 points together. Even if the mean went up, if the median stayed the same, it may be an effect of two scores changing a lot, so both should be reported to avoid misunderstanding.
y-m-31-03.s.s3.model.1: I will write that the median stayed at 70 points, and add that the mean went up because of changes in one or two scores. This is because most students' scores did not change.
y-m-31-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that centered on the median instead of the mean but explained the cause of the change in the mean.

y-m-31-04.title: What can we say for certain when we only know the mean and the standard deviation?
y-m-31-04.topic: What the mean and standard deviation alone can tell
y-m-31-04.goal: Tell apart what can be said for certain, what is possible but not certain, and what you need to know more about when only the mean and standard deviation are given, and find impossible values yourself.
y-m-31-04.material: The mean of a math test (0 to 100 points, scores are integers) taken by the 30 students of one class in grade 9 of a school is 70 points, and the standard deviation is 5 points. The individual scores are not known. These 30 students of the class are all of the people surveyed, so the variance (= 25) is the value found by dividing by 30. So if you add up all the squared deviations of the 30 students, it is 25×30=750.
y-m-31-04.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-31-04.thinking.1: Showing with a counterexample that something is not 'necessarily true'
y-m-31-04.thinking.2: Filtering out impossible cases by reasoning
y-m-31-04.prereq.0: The meaning of mean, deviation, variance, and standard deviation (grade 9). Since the variance is the mean of the squared deviations, the relation (sum of squared deviations) = (number of data values) × (variance)
y-m-31-04.prereq.1: A squared deviation is always 0 or more
y-m-31-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the statements that you can say are necessarily true from only the information that the mean is 70 points and the standard deviation is 5 points.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each statement, make one or two lists of scores by yourself that make the statement false, and check whether the mean and the sum of squared deviations fit.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether one student's squared deviation can be greater than the sum of squared deviations (750).
y-m-31-04.s.s1.o.a: The scores of the students in this class are all 65 points or more and 75 points or less.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.r.a: A standard deviation of 5 does not mean 'every student is within 5 points of the mean'. Even if some are farther away, the standard deviation can still be 5.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.o.b: There is at least one student in this class with exactly 70 points.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.r.b: A mean of 70 does not mean there must be a student who got 70. The mean can be 70 even with only 60 points and 80 points.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.o.c: There is at least one student who got a score higher than 70 points.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.r.c: The standard deviation is not 0, so the scores cannot all be 70 points, and the mean is 70, so if there is a student lower than 70 there must also be a higher one. You connected the meaning of the mean with the fact that the standard deviation is not 0.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.o.d: The median of this class is 70 points.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.r.d: The mean and the median can be different. From the mean and standard deviation alone you cannot know the score in the middle position.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.o.e: There is not a single student in this class with 40 points or less.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.r.e: If the deviation is 30 or more, the squared deviation of one student alone is 900 or more. It exceeds the total 750, so it is impossible. This is good reasoning that used the fact that the sum of squared deviations is fixed.
y-m-31-04.s.s1.explain: The sum of squared deviations is fixed at 750, so one student's squared deviation cannot exceed 750. At 40 points the deviation is -30 and the square is 900, so it is impossible. Also, if the standard deviation is not 0, the scores cannot all be the same, and since the mean is 70, there is a student higher than 70. The median, the existence of a student with 70 points, and 'all are 65 to 75 points' cannot be said from this information alone.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different scores that are certain not to be possible as one student's score in this class. (Integers from 0 to 100)
y-m-31-04.s.s2.hint.0: Decide a candidate score and first check whether the square of its difference from 70 (the deviation) exceeds 750.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.hint.1: For scores like 45 points and 60 points, test whether you can make a list of scores that satisfies the mean 70 and the standard deviation 5 even with such a student.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer from 0 to 100.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Make the score an integer from 0 to 100.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.ok.c2: If there were a student with this score, the sum of squared deviations 750 and the mean 70 could not be satisfied at the same time.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.fail.c2: This score is possible in this class. There can be a student with that score, and you can make a list of scores in which the other students also fit the mean and the sum of squared deviations.
y-m-31-04.s.s2.explain: One student's squared deviation cannot exceed 750, and the deviations of the other 29 students must sum to cancel that student's deviation, so in practice it cannot exceed about 725. So 43 points or less and 97 points or more are impossible. 20 points, 35 points, and 100 points are examples that are easily filtered out, and 43 points and 97 points are boundary examples that need more careful calculation. On the other hand, 45 points is possible: if one student has 45, five have 75, and twenty-four have 70, the mean is 70 and the standard deviation is 5.
y-m-31-04.s.s3.prompt: A friend said, 'The standard deviation is 5 points, so every student in this class is between 65 points and 75 points.' Write, with a concrete example, why this statement is not necessarily right, and also write what you would need to know more to check whether it is right.
y-m-31-04.s.s3.hint.0: Decide one list of scores in which some students are outside 65 to 75 points, and check whether the mean and the sum of squared deviations of that list fit.
y-m-31-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write what score information you would need to see to say 'every student is within that range'.
y-m-31-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. It is not necessarily right. For example, ...
y-m-31-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the example I gave, did I check that the mean 70 and the standard deviation 5 really fit?
y-m-31-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I use the fact that one counterexample is enough to break the word 'every student'?
y-m-31-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I write concretely what information would let us check this statement?
y-m-31-04.s.s3.model.0: It is not necessarily right. For example, if one student has 45 points, five have 75 points, and the other 24 have 70 points, the mean is 70 and the standard deviation is 5, but there is a student with 45 points. To check, you need to know the students' individual scores or the lowest and highest scores.
y-m-31-04.s.s3.model.1: The standard deviation is only a representative size of how far the scores are from the mean. It is fine for some students to be outside 65 to 75, so you cannot say everyone is inside. You need to look at the score distribution (a frequency table) to know.

y-m-31-05.title: If both standard deviations are 6, are they spread out equally?
y-m-31-05.topic: Comparing the spread of data with different units
y-m-31-05.goal: Judge whether the standard deviation numbers of two data sets with different units can be compared directly, and explain what method and conditions are needed to compare them.
y-m-31-05.material: In the school nurse's office, the heights and weights of 20 students in the same class were measured. The height has a mean of 160 cm and a standard deviation of 6 cm, and the weight has a mean of 52 kg and a standard deviation of 6 kg. Jihu said, 'The standard deviations are both 6, so height and weight are spread out to the same degree!'
y-m-31-05.thinking.0: Judging while considering the meaning of the numbers (the units)
y-m-31-05.thinking.1: Checking a claim with new information
y-m-31-05.thinking.2: Proposing a comparison method and its limits
y-m-31-05.prereq.0: The larger the standard deviation, the more widely the data is spread around the mean (grade 9)
y-m-31-05.prereq.1: The relation between the length units m and cm (1 m = 100 cm)
y-m-31-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most fitting thought about Jihu's statement.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.hint.0: In the height data and the weight data, write what unit each standard deviation of 6 is measured in.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.hint.1: If you write the height in m, calculate what the mean and the standard deviation each become.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.o.a: The standard deviations are both 6, so we can say the two data sets are spread out equally.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.r.a: The number of a standard deviation changes with the unit. You cannot directly read the 6 in the different units cm and kg as the same value.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.o.b: The height data, which has the larger mean, is spread by 6, so height is spread out more than weight.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.r.b: A larger mean does not mean a larger spread. Rather, compared with the mean, how large 6 is can look different.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.o.c: One is in cm and the other in kg, so it is hard to directly set the number 6 side by side and compare.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.r.c: You pointed out that standard deviations of quantities with different units should not be compared by their numbers alone.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.o.d: Weight, where 6 takes up a larger share of the mean, can be seen as relatively more spread out.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.r.d: This is a method of comparing by the share relative to the mean (6÷160 and 6÷52). If you set it as an agreement, it is a valid comparison, but it is not comparing 'the standard deviation numbers themselves'.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.explain: It is hard to compare the numbers of the standard deviations of two data sets with different units as they are. This is because the numbers change when the unit changes. If you set a separate standard that removes the effect of the unit, such as the share relative to the mean, you can compare them.
y-m-31-05.s.s1.acc.0: Comparing by the size relative to the mean (6÷160 is about 3.8% and 6÷52 is about 11.5%) is a valid method. However, this does not compare the standard deviation numbers directly; it sets a different standard called 'the share relative to the mean'.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.prompt: This is new information. When the height was written in m instead of cm, the mean became 1.6 m and the standard deviation 0.06 m. The weight stays the same, with a mean of 52 kg and a standard deviation of 6 kg. What can you say now?
y-m-31-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write what one student's height of 160 cm becomes in m, and think about whether the same thing happens to all the students.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what the standard deviation would be if the weight were written in g.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.o.a: The standard deviation 0.06 is much smaller than 6, so the height is hardly spread at all and the weight is spread much more.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.r.a: Check whether the conclusion changes just by changing the unit of the same height data. If you look at the numbers only, the conclusion flips every time you change the unit.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.o.b: Only the unit was changed and the spread is the same, so you must not judge by setting the standard deviation numbers side by side.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.r.b: You pointed out that even if the unit changes, the spread of the data is the same and only the standard deviation number changes to fit the unit.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.o.c: The calculation is wrong. I think the standard deviation should stay 6 even if the unit changes.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.r.c: If you change length from cm to m, all values are divided by 100, so both the mean and the standard deviation are divided by 100. 0.06 m is the right value.
y-m-31-05.s.s2.explain: Only cm was changed to m, and the heights of the 20 students are the same, so the spread is the same. But the standard deviation number changed from 6 cm to 0.06 m. So if you directly compare the standard deviation numbers of different units, the conclusion flips depending on how you write the unit.
y-m-31-05.s.s3.prompt: You want to compare which of the height data and the weight data is more spread out. Propose one method of comparing, and also write the limits or conditions of that method.
y-m-31-05.s.s3.hint.0: Think, by comparing with the mean, about whether there is a way to turn the standard deviation of the height data into a number without a unit.
y-m-31-05.s.s3.hint.1: Test whether the method I proposed gives the same result even if the height is written in m.
y-m-31-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my method keep the same conclusion even if the unit changes?
y-m-31-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I think of even one case in which my method would not work well?
y-m-31-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I test the method once by putting in numbers?
y-m-31-05.s.s3.model.0: You can compare by the ratio of each data set's standard deviation divided by its mean. For height it is 6÷160 and for weight it is 6÷52. However, this method does not work well for data whose mean is close to 0 or that has negative values.
y-m-31-05.s.s3.model.1: Let's compare within the same unit. For example, put the height data of students in another class and this class's height data both in cm and compare the standard deviations. The limit is that data of different kinds, like height and weight, cannot be compared by this method.
y-m-31-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: A method that changes what is compared instead of comparing data of different kinds.

y-m-31-06.title: A salary job ad: is it fine to use only the mean?
y-m-31-06.topic: Choosing a representative value and the text that announces it
y-m-31-06.goal: Think about the impression the mean gives readers when the data has an extremely large value, and choose or rewrite the representative value and sentences so readers are not misled.
y-m-31-06.material: The snack shop 'Byeolbit Bunsik' wants to post a job ad for hiring staff. The monthly salaries (만 원) of the current 6 employees are 200, 200, 210, 220, 230, 860 (860 is the manager's salary). The draft of the ad is below.
y-m-31-06.thinking.0: Evaluating the impression a sentence gives the reader
y-m-31-06.thinking.1: Choosing a representative value that fits the shape of the data
y-m-31-06.thinking.2: Rewriting a sentence for the reader
y-m-31-06.prereq.0: The meaning of mean, median, and mode and how to find them (grades 7 to 8)
y-m-31-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line of this ad that is easy for an applicant to misunderstand.
y-m-31-06.s.s1.hint.0: Arrange the 6 salaries by size and count how many employees receive less than the mean of 320만 원.
y-m-31-06.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether each line is 'a statement announcing a calculation result' or 'a statement about what the reader comes to believe from that result'.
y-m-31-06.s.s1.line.0: Byeolbit Bunsik is looking for staff to work with.
y-m-31-06.s.s1.line.1: The monthly salaries (만 원) of the current 6 employees are 200, 200, 210, 220, 230, 860.
y-m-31-06.s.s1.line.2: The average monthly salary of employees is 320만 원.
y-m-31-06.s.s1.line.3: If you join our shop, anyone can receive close to 320만 원.
y-m-31-06.s.s1.line.4: If you are interested, please contact the shop.
y-m-31-06.s.s1.explain: The line that is easy to misunderstand is line 4. The mean of 320만 원 in line 3 is a correctly calculated value, but 5 out of 6 people receive less than 320만 원. One person's 860만 원 pulled the mean up. Line 4 makes the mean read like 'an amount anyone can receive'. If you chose line 3, look at it together with line 4 and see that the calculation is right but the problem is that the mean does not represent the salaries of most employees.
y-m-31-06.s.s2.prompt: As a number to put in the ad, which can an applicant read with the least misunderstanding?
y-m-31-06.s.s2.hint.0: Arrange the 6 salaries by size and check between the 3rd and 4th values.
y-m-31-06.s.s2.hint.1: Imagine, for each option, how the reader will guess 'the salary I will get'.
y-m-31-06.s.s2.o.a: Write the average employee salary of 320만 원 together with how that value was found
y-m-31-06.s.s2.r.a: The mean is a correct value, but even if you state the method, the reader cannot know that 5 people get less than the mean.
y-m-31-06.s.s2.o.b: Write the highest salary, 860만 원, with big emphasis
y-m-31-06.s.s2.r.b: It is just an eye-catching value. It is an amount only one person receives, so it does not tell the salaries of most employees.
y-m-31-06.s.s2.o.c: Write only 200만 원, the salary that appears most often, as the representative value
y-m-31-06.s.s2.r.c: It tells you that two people receive that salary, but you cannot know the other employees' salaries, and it only shows the lowest side.
y-m-31-06.s.s2.o.d: Write the median of 215만 원 together with the range of the salaries (200 to 860)
y-m-31-06.s.s2.r.d: By giving the middle salary and the range of salaries together, it makes up for what the mean misses.
y-m-31-06.s.s2.explain: In this data, one person's salary is much larger, so the mean (320) is higher than most employees (200 to 230). If you give the median (215), the middle value, together with the lowest and highest values (200, 860), the reader can guess the actual distribution.
y-m-31-06.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite line 4 so that applicants are not misled. Include at least one salary number.
y-m-31-06.s.s3.hint.0: First sum up in one sentence how many of the 6 salaries are in which range.
y-m-31-06.s.s3.hint.1: Read your corrected sentence from the point of view of someone seeing it for the first time, and guess 'about how much I would probably get'.
y-m-31-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: About how much does the reader guess 'the salary I will get'?
y-m-31-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Which of the mean, median, and range did I use, and why did I think that value fits this data?
y-m-31-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is it a sentence that is not false but reduces misunderstanding?
y-m-31-06.s.s3.model.0: The middle value of the 6 current employees' salaries is 215만 원, the highest salary is 860만 원, and the lowest salary is 200만 원. Most employees receive in the 200만 원 range.
y-m-31-06.s.s3.model.1: The average employee salary is 320만 원, but one person receives 860만 원, which makes the average high. The other 5 people receive 200 to 230만 원.
y-m-31-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: A method that uses the mean but states why that value came out high.

y-m-31-07.title: It came out as no correlation, but is there really no relationship at all?
y-m-31-07.topic: Relationships in a scatter plot that are not a straight line
y-m-31-07.goal: Learn that 'no correlation' means 'no straight-line tendency', and make data that has a non-linear relationship yourself to rebut a friend's conclusion.
y-m-31-07.material: 8 students were asked about their sleep time last night (x, hours) and their focus in class today (y, 0 to 10 points). (x, y) are (4, 3), (5, 5), (6, 8), (7, 9), (8, 9), (9, 8), (10, 5), (11, 3). These 8 points have no tendency to lean to one side (focus does not overall rise or fall as sleep time gets longer). A friend, Hayun, said, 'There is no correlation, so sleep time has no relationship at all with focus.'
y-m-31-07.thinking.0: Checking the scope of a claim (a straight-line tendency vs any relationship)
y-m-31-07.thinking.1: Making new data that fits the conditions
y-m-31-07.prereq.0: Scatter plots and positive correlation, negative correlation, and no correlation (middle school grade 8 to 9 level)
y-m-31-07.prereq.1: Reading ordered pairs like (sleep time, focus) as points
y-m-31-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most fitting thought about Hayun's conclusion.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.hint.0: Read the sleep times in order from 4 hours to 11 hours and write how the focus changes.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.hint.1: Find the sleep time with the highest focus and the sleep time with the lowest focus and compare them.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.o.a: 'No correlation' only means there is no tendency to lean; a relationship of another shape can exist.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.r.a: You pointed out that 'no correlation' does not mean the same as 'no relationship'.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.o.b: I think that if the points do not form a straight-line shape, you can say there is no relationship at all between the two values.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.r.b: Two values can have a relationship even in a shape that is not a straight line. Read the numbers in the table in order.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.o.c: I think focus keeps getting higher the longer the sleep time, so there should be a correlation.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.r.c: Read the points. The focus for 10 and 11 hours of sleep is low. Focus does not keep going up for long sleep times.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.o.d: There are only 8 points, so I think you cannot say anything at all about whether there is a relationship between the two values.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.r.d: Even 8 points show a clear shape (high at middle sleep times and low at both ends). Being a small data set is a reason to be careful, not a sign that nothing can be said.
y-m-31-07.s.s1.explain: 'No correlation' means the points have no tendency (a straight-line shape) leaning in one direction. This data has a clear relationship: students who sleep too little or too much have low focus and students who sleep an appropriate amount have high focus. Seen as a straight line there is no tendency, but that does not mean the two values are unrelated.
y-m-31-07.s.s2.prompt: Make data for 3 new students that continues the same pattern. Sleep time x is an integer from 3 to 12 and focus y is an integer from 0 to 10. Enter 3 students with different sleep times so that 'if sleep time is 5 hours or less or 10 hours or more, focus is 5 points or less, and if it is 6 to 9 hours, focus is 7 points or more'.
y-m-31-07.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the sleep time, then check which range (5 hours or less, 6 to 9 hours, 10 hours or more) that time is in.
y-m-31-07.s.s2.hint.1: Depending on the range, decide whether the focus must be 5 points or less or 7 points or more, then choose a score within that range.
y-m-31-07.s.s2.ok.c1: Sleep time and focus are integers within the range.
y-m-31-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Make sleep time an integer from 3 to 12 and focus an integer from 0 to 10.
y-m-31-07.s.s2.fail.c2: It does not fit the pattern. If the sleep time is 5 hours or less or 10 hours or more, the focus must be 5 points or less, and if it is 6 to 9 hours, 7 points or more.
y-m-31-07.s.s2.explain: For example, (3, 2), (7, 10), and (12, 1) fit the pattern. Even when points are added where focus is low if sleep is too short or too long and high if appropriate, the points do not lean to one side. Data with this pattern can come out as no correlation, but the two values clearly have a relationship.
y-m-31-07.s.s3.prompt: How would you explain it to Hayun? Using the data above as an example, write how 'no correlation' and 'no relationship' are different.
y-m-31-07.s.s3.hint.0: Separate the 'no correlation' part and the 'no relationship at all' part of Hayun's statement and check whether each is right.
y-m-31-07.s.s3.hint.1: In the table, write the sleep times of the points with high focus and of the points with low focus.
y-m-31-07.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. Hayun, if you look at the points, ...
y-m-31-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I tell apart how far Hayun's statement is right and where it becomes an overgeneralization?
y-m-31-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I check whether the values I gave match the values in the table?
y-m-31-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can the explanation be understood even without the word 'straight line'?
y-m-31-07.s.s3.model.0: Hayun, no correlation means the points do not lean to one side. But students who slept 7 to 8 hours have a focus of 9 points and students who slept 4 hours or 11 hours have 3 points, so there is a clear relationship between sleep time and focus.
y-m-31-07.s.s3.model.1: Not being a straight-line shape does not mean there is no relationship. If you sleep too little or too much, focus is low, and if you sleep an appropriate amount, it is high, so you can see a pattern that is high in the middle. This relationship just does not show up well as a correlation.
y-m-31-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that separated correlation and relationship and used the pattern of the data as evidence.

y-m-31-08.title: If we combine the means of two classes, is it the overall mean?
y-m-31-08.topic: The mean of two groups combined
y-m-31-08.goal: Learn that the means of two groups alone cannot determine the combined mean, say what information (the number of students) is also needed, and make class-size combinations that fit the conditions yourself.
y-m-31-08.material: The mean of class A is 70 points and the mean of class B is 80 points (same test, with at least 1 student in each class). You want to know the mean of all the students of the two classes combined. Soyul said, 'The mean of the two class means, 75 points, is the overall mean.' You do not yet know the number of students in the two classes.
y-m-31-08.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-31-08.thinking.1: Making several cases that satisfy the conditions
y-m-31-08.thinking.2: Saying the conditions under which a generalization (the mean of two means) holds
y-m-31-08.prereq.0: The meaning of mean: (total sum) ÷ (number of data values) (grade 7)
y-m-31-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the fitting explanation about Soyul's statement and the combined overall mean.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put in one number at a time and compare how the total score sum differs when the numbers of students in A and B are equal and when A has many more.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.hint.1: Write what you can find out by multiplying each class's mean by its number of students.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.o.a: I think 75 points, the middle of the two means, necessarily becomes the overall mean of the two classes combined.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.r.a: If the numbers of students in the two classes are different, their effects on the mean are different too. If one class is much bigger, the overall mean gets closer to that class.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.o.b: The overall mean is between 70 points and 80 points, but you need to know the number of students to know the exact value.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out together that the combined mean lies between the two means and that the exact value needs information about the number of students.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.o.c: Even without knowing the number of students, class B's mean is higher, so the overall mean is necessarily higher than 75 points.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.r.c: Even if class B's mean is higher, if class A has far more students, it can be lower than 75 points. Look at the number of students.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.o.d: I think that even without knowing the number of students, you can calculate the overall mean exactly with only 70 and 80.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.r.d: From the means alone you cannot know each class's sum of scores. You can know the sum of scores only by multiplying the mean by the number of students.
y-m-31-08.s.s1.explain: Each class's sum of scores is (mean)×(number of students), so the overall mean is (70×number in A + 80×number in B)÷(total number). It is 75 points only when the numbers are equal. Depending on which side has more students, it gets closer to 70 or closer to 80, but it is always between 70 and 80.
y-m-31-08.s.s2.prompt: Decide the number of students a in class A and b in class B (both integers from 1 to 40) so that the combined overall mean is from 72 points to 74 points. Make 3 cases with different ratios of the numbers of students. (e.g. 20 and 10, and 10 and 5 have the same ratio, so count them as one.)
y-m-31-08.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether A should have more or B should have more, and which class must have more students for the overall mean to go toward the side closer to 70.
y-m-31-08.s.s2.hint.1: Decide a pair of numbers of students, calculate (70×a+80×b)÷(a+b), and check that it is between 72 and 74. Remember that pairs with the same ratio are counted as one.
y-m-31-08.s.s2.var.a: Number of students in class A
y-m-31-08.s.s2.var.b: Number of students in class B
y-m-31-08.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of students are integers within the range.
y-m-31-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Make the numbers of students integers from 1 to 40.
y-m-31-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The combined mean is from 72 points to 74 points.
y-m-31-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The combined mean is not from 72 points to 74 points. Check (70×a+80×b)÷(a+b).
y-m-31-08.s.s2.explain: If class A has 1.5 times to 4 times as many students as class B, the combined mean is 72 to 74 points. (30, 10) has a mean of 72.5, (20, 10) is about 73.3, and (6, 4) is exactly 74. (10, 10) has a mean of 75 and (10, 30) has 77.5, so they are outside the range.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.prompt: Write when Soyul's statement 'the mean of the two means is the overall mean' is right and when it is not.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.hint.0: For the case where the numbers of students in the two classes are the same and the case where they are different, write the total score sum as (mean)×(number of students) and compare.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.hint.1: Put in an example of numbers of students, like 20 and 10, and calculate the overall mean directly.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. When the numbers of students in the two classes are ..., it is right, and when ..., it is not.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I say both the case where it is right and the case where it is not?
y-m-31-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I give a number example (e.g. 20 and 10)?
y-m-31-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I explain in line with the meaning 'the overall mean is the sum of scores divided by the total number of students'?
y-m-31-08.s.s3.model.0: If the two classes have the same number of students, 75 points is right. But if the numbers are different, it gets closer to the mean of the class with more students. For example, with 30 students in class A and 10 in class B, (2100+800)÷40=72.5, which is not 75.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.model.1: Only when classes A and B have exactly the same number of students is the mean of the two means the overall mean. If the numbers of students are different, the overall mean leans toward the mean of the class with more students, so it is wrong.
y-m-31-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that explained the reason in words without a number example.
